meta.title: Amharic A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Amharic → English (see the Amharic, recall the meaning) and English → Amharic (see an English meaning, recall the Amharic). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Amharic, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 118 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the months of the Ethiopian calendar, clothes, work and jobs, relatives and the stages of life, feelings, travel, the countryside and the weather, the body and health, food and the kitchen, the things of a home, talking and deciding, the everyday verbs of doing, describing things, and the feasts and the faith — and the other 632 are the commonest remaining words of the Amharic Wikipedia, counted by the WHOLE word: Amharic writes its prepositions and endings onto the word (ቤት 'house', ቤቱ 'the house', በቤቱ 'in the house'), so those forms are added together. That corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (history, government, religion), and verbs are counted less well than nouns, so they rank lower than they are used. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and some of the commonest are missing from it (አዎ 'yes', እና 'and', ግን 'but', ለምን 'why', ሄደ 'to go'). Every word is in the Ethiopic script (fidäl), as Amharic is written; the Fidäl deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters. Beneath it is Wiktionary's romanisation, which also marks the doubled consonants the script leaves unwritten. A verb is shown by its dictionary form, the past 'he did' (ገዛ 'he bought', taught as 'to buy'), with its infinitive where Wiktionary gives one; a few verbs Wiktionary has only as an infinitive are taught by that (መምጣት 'to come'). A noun shows its gender, plural and definite form where Wiktionary has them. Several Amharic letters are said alike (ሀ ሐ ኀ, ሰ ሠ, አ ዐ, ጸ ፀ), so many words have two or three spellings; the card heads with the one the Amharic Wikipedia uses most and names the others. Example sentences are few: 24 of the 750 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 250 Amharic sentences with a translation; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have an Amharic voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Amharic Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
